news.title: Fake FBI Agents Are Calling — Hang Up and Check
news.excerpt: Crooks are making fake calls, saying they are FBI, DEA, or Secret Service agents. They make a real agency's phone number show up on your screen and use a real agent's name, then push you to move your money to keep it "safe." The FBI says never send money to anyone claiming to be a federal agent. If this happens to you, it's a scam — hang up and call the agency yourself at a number you look up. I've had two customers ask me about calls like this just this week.

news.title: Fake Bank Fraud Alerts Want Your Money
news.excerpt: Someone calls or texts pretending to be your bank. They say there is suspicious activity and you must move your money to a "safe" account right now. That is the whole scam — and it is surging again this week. Real banks never ask you to move money to protect it. Hang up, then call your bank yourself using the number on your card or your last statement. I tell every customer the same thing: check first, every time.

news.title: Fake Recall Texts Want Your Card
news.excerpt: Scammers are texting and emailing that something you bought was recalled for safety and that you are owed money back. Tap the link and it asks you to sign in or type a card number — that is the whole trick, and it is spreading fast right now. Real recalls never arrive as a link in a surprise message. Check the product yourself, free, at cpsc.gov/recalls, or open the store's app and look at your orders. My rule is simple: don't click, check it yourself.

news.title: An Emergency Apple Fix for a Flaw Hackers Are Already Using
news.excerpt: Apple rushed out an emergency update this week for a flaw hackers are already using against Apple computers. The fix stops a harmful file — one you might open from an email or a download — from running hidden code. The real repair is free from Apple, so ignore any pop-up telling you to call a number; that is a scam. It takes two minutes: open the Apple menu, click System Settings, then General, then Software Update. I've seen computers sit months behind — please update today.

news.title: A Fake \"You're Invited\" Email Is the New Way In
news.excerpt: Scammers are breaking into regular email accounts and sending fake invitations — a birthday party, a fundraiser, a wedding — from someone you actually know. Click "view the invitation" and it asks you to sign in with Google, Apple, or Microsoft; that login screen is fake, and the password you type goes straight to the crooks. A real invitation never asks you to log in just to see it. I tell folks to check with the sender by a quick call first.

posts.title: Sound and look better on video calls — a Logitech webcam with a built-in microphone is about 40 dollars at logitech.com or Amazon
posts.summary: Buy a Logitech webcam — the C270 is about 40 dollars and the C920 is about 60 — from logitech.com, Amazon, or Walmart. Plug the USB cable into your computer and you're done; there's nothing to install on Windows or a Mac. You get a much sharper picture and a microphone that doesn't echo, so family, doctors, and work calls can actually see and hear you.
posts.truth:
Most people don't realize the camera built into a laptop was the cheapest part the maker could buy. That's why you look dim, grainy, and washed out while the person you're talking to looks fine — they have a better camera, not a better face. The honest answer is that a 40-dollar webcam is one of the biggest quality-of-life upgrades a home computer can get, and it plugs into a USB port in five seconds.

I see this all the time: a customer apologizes for "looking bad" on every video call. It's never them. It's the camera.

posts.title: Nobody from the government will call or text you demanding money — report it free at ic3.gov, the FBI's own complaint site
posts.summary: If someone calls or texts claiming to be the police, the FBI, the IRS, or Social Security and says you owe money, missed jury duty, or have a warrant out, hang up. Real government offices do not call demanding payment, and they never ask for gift cards, cash, or cryptocurrency. If it already happened to you, file a free report at ic3.gov — that's the FBI's own complaint website. The FBI says scammers ran this exact play thousands of times and stole more than a billion and a half dollars from people between January 2025 and July 2026.
posts.truth:
Most people don't realize the scariest part of this scam isn't the phone call — it's that the caller knows your name, your town, and sometimes the last four of your Social Security number. That's why it feels real. The honest answer is that no amount of information they read back to you changes one simple fact: the government does not collect debts by phone, and it will never tell you to keep it secret from your family.

I see this all the time: a customer comes in shaken because "the sheriff's office" called about a warrant and told them not to tell anyone. The moment someone tells you not to tell your family, you're talking to a criminal.

posts.title: Your hard drive warns you before it dies — CrystalDiskInfo is the free health checker at crystalmark.info
posts.summary: Download CrystalDiskInfo free from crystalmark.info (it's the Crystal Dew World site), open it, and look at the big word at the top of the window. A blue Good means your drive is healthy. A yellow Caution or a red Bad means it's on its way out, and you should copy your pictures and documents off it today. It's free, it works with no internet connection, and reading it takes about a minute.
posts.truth:
Most people don't realize that a hard drive almost never dies without warning. It starts making small mistakes long before it stops working, and it keeps a private log of those mistakes that this free program reads for you in plain English. A failing drive is one of the very few computer problems that is truly urgent — every day you wait is one day closer to losing every photo and every family video at once.

I see this all the time: a customer brings in a slow computer, and the real problem is a drive that's been quietly telling on itself for months. Nothing feels broken, so nobody checks. That's exactly why I open it and check every customer who walks in — a one-minute look now is worth more than any recovery bill later.

posts.title: Chrome now asks before opening an unsafe website — update yours free at chrome://settings/help
posts.summary: Chrome is turning on a safer way to browse this month: it tries the secure version of a site first, and if the site can't do secure, it stops and asks you before opening it — you'll see a warning instead of walking in blind. To be sure you have it, open Chrome, click the three dots in the top-right corner, then Help, then About Google Chrome. It updates itself in about a minute. Not sure you have Chrome? Go to google.com/chrome and click Download. Free, from Google.
posts.truth:
A little padlock in the address bar is the whole difference between a private note and a postcard anyone can read. You don't need to understand the technical part at all — you just need the browser to slow you down for one second before you type a password or a card number into a page that isn't locked. That one pause is what catches the mistake.

I see this all the time: a customer types their bank login on a page that looked normal, and only the tiny "Not secure" text said otherwise. Starting this month Chrome does the noticing for you. When it asks, the safe answer is almost always to go back and try the site again by typing the address fresh, or to skip it entirely and call the business instead.

posts.title: Firefox just got a cleaner new look that can tuck your tabs down the left side — update free at firefox.com
posts.summary: Open Firefox, click the Menu button (the three lines in the top-right corner), then Help, then About Firefox — it checks for the new version and installs it for you in about two minutes. Don't have Firefox yet? Go to firefox.com and click Download; it's free and it's made by Mozilla.
posts.truth:
Most people don't realize how much of their day lives inside one square of glass — email, banking, the pharmacy, the grandkids' photos. And yet the program you look through all day is the one people update last. An old browser is one of the easiest ways for a stranger to get onto your computer, because the fixes for the tricks they use are sitting right there in the update you keep putting off.

I see this all the time: someone tells me their computer is "fine" — until we look at the browser and it hasn't been touched in two years. The new Firefox look is nice, but the real reason to update today is the security that rides along with it.

posts.title: Type and click without touching the keyboard — Windows Voice Access is built into Windows 11, free at Settings > Accessibility > Speech
posts.summary: Open Settings > Accessibility > Speech and turn on Voice access. Then just talk: say "open my email," "click Save," or "type Dear Mary" and Windows does it for you. It's built into Windows 11, costs nothing, needs no account, and works even without internet. If your hands ache, your keyboard is acting up, or you'd simply rather talk than type, this turns your computer into a hands-free machine.
posts.truth:
Most people don't realize Windows already has a full voice-control feature — they picture expensive software or a subscription, so they never look. It's sitting right there in Settings. It won't read your mind, and you do have to speak a little clearly, but for anyone whose hands hurt or who types slowly, it's the difference between fighting the computer and just using it.

I see this all the time: someone with arthritis or a recovering wrist injury, quietly struggling every day. Two minutes in Settings changes their whole afternoon.

posts.title: Windows 11's new Point-in-Time Restore can undo a bad update or a wrong click — turn it on free at Settings > System > Recovery
posts.summary: Open Settings > System > Recovery, click Point-in-time restore, then View or edit, and turn it on. From then on, Windows quietly keeps a snapshot of your whole computer — your programs, your settings, and your own files — so if a bad update or a wrong click wrecks things, you can roll the whole machine back to how it was this morning. It's free, it's built into Windows 11, and turning it on takes about two minutes.
posts.truth:
Most people don't realize that the old Windows "restore point" never saved your files — it only reset Windows itself, so your pictures and documents stayed broken. This new one is different: it captures your personal files too, and it keeps a few days of history. The honest answer is that this is the closest thing to a real undo button Windows has ever had, and almost nobody has turned it on.

I see this all the time: a customer installs something, or an update goes sideways, and the machine won't behave. With this on, that's a five-minute rollback instead of a reinstall and a bill. It won't replace a real backup, but it will save you a very bad afternoon.

posts.title: Using the same password everywhere? Google's free Password Checkup at passwords.google.com/checkup finds the weak ones
posts.summary: Open your browser and go to passwords.google.com/checkup. Sign in with your Google account and click Checkup. It shows you every saved password that is too weak, reused on more than one website, or already leaked in a data breach — and it walks you through changing each one, site by site. It's free, it's built into your Google account, and there's nothing to download.
posts.truth:
Most people don't realize that the danger isn't one website getting hacked — it's that the same password opens the same door everywhere. When one company has a leak, criminals take that email-and-password pair and try it on your bank, your email, and your Facebook within minutes. The honest answer is that you don't need a different password for all fifty sites you visit; you need a different one for the five that matter most, and this free check tells you exactly which five are in trouble.

I see this all the time: a customer swears they were "hacked," and what actually happened is that one old password was reused on a site that leaked years ago. Nobody ever told them. A five-minute checkup would have caught it.

posts.title: ChatGPT is now free inside Microsoft Word — get the add-in free at chatgpt.com/apps/word or Word's Insert > Get Add-ins
posts.summary: Open Microsoft Word, click Insert at the top, then Get Add-ins, and search ChatGPT to install it — free. (You can also go to chatgpt.com/apps/word and click Install.) A ChatGPT panel appears on the right side of your document. You can ask it to fix a sentence, shorten a paragraph, write a first draft of a thank-you note or a complaint letter, or explain a word in a contract. You only need a free ChatGPT account, and the free plan includes a set amount of use each month.
posts.truth:
The hardest part of writing is the blank page, not the writing. You should never let a computer send anything for you without reading it first, but there is nothing wrong with using one to get you unstuck. A rough note becomes a clean paragraph in seconds, and you still decide if it sounds like you.

I see this all the time: a customer needs a letter to an insurance company, a landlord, or the school, and they sit there stuck for an hour. With ChatGPT right inside Word, you type "help me write a polite letter asking for a refund, here are the facts" and it gives you a starting point you can edit. My one rule: never put your Social Security number, bank numbers, or passwords into any AI chat. Everything else is fair game.

posts.title: Someone using your Google account? Google's free Security Checkup at myaccount.google.com/security-checkup shows every device signed in
posts.summary: Open myaccount.google.com/security-checkup in your browser, sign in with your Google account, and follow the short list it shows you. It reviews the devices signed in to your account, the apps that have access to it, and any password it thinks is weak or reused — and it walks you through fixing each one. No download, no cost, about two minutes.
posts.truth:
Most people don't realize that when a stranger gets your Google password, they don't just read your email — they quietly sit there, and Gmail is the key that resets the password on almost everything else you own. The honest answer is that you cannot hear someone logging into your account from a thousand miles away, but you can look. That is all this page is: a free look at who is inside, and a button to shut the door.

I see this all the time: a customer swears nothing is wrong, and then we open this page and find a device they don't recognize signed in from another state. Sometimes it's harmless — an old phone they forgot about. Sometimes it isn't. Either way, you want to be the one who finds it first, not your bank.
